To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the endogenous oxidative stress and antioxidant defense systems in tumours are determined by the status mitochondrial, metabolic, hypoxia and inherent enzymatic and non-enzymic antioxidant defense systems, influence tumour growth as well as respond to anticancer therapy.

(i) MCTS offer an excellent in vivo like model to study oxidative stress in tumour cells, (ii) ROS generation by certain chemotherapeutic agents and metabolic inhibitors in MCTS induces apoptosis and necrosis and (iii) ROS generation in MCTS enhances the efficacy of anticancer agents.

the MCTS model is an excellent in vitro model for studying the endogenous and induced oxidative stresses in tumours and their implications in therapy, and that this model is ideally suited for developing and evaluating novel therapeutic strategies based on generation of oxidative stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (i) to investigate the role of endogenous and induced oxidative stresses in MCTS, (ii) to identify the molecular targets that can be exploited for enhancing the therapeutic efficiency of anticancer agents, (iii) to design new strategies to overcome resistance against anticancer agents, particularly in MCTS and (iv) to explore the role of oxidative stresses in the treatment of tumours in vivo, using animal models.
the role of oxidative and nitrosative stress in tumour cells and its implication for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.
developing novel therapies and therapeutics based on oxidative stress in tumour cells, particularly using multi-cellular tumours spheroid (MCTS) model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MCTS offer a unique and excellent in vitro model system for studying the endogenous and induced oxidative stresses, which could be exploited for developing therapies and therapeutics for tumours.
the use of MCTS is a very promising approach for understanding the role of endogenous and induced oxidative stresses in tumour growth and treatment and for designing novel therapies.

the MCTS are an excellent in vitro model system that mimics oxidative stress in tumour cells, thereby offering an opportunity to study the responses of tumours to oxidative stress, which could be used to design novel therapeutic approaches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

MCTS can be used to study the endogenous and induced oxidative responses of tumours in vivo and can be exploited for developing novel therapies and therapeutics that are based on oxidative stress in tumour cells.

MCTS are excellent in vitro models for studying the endogenous and induced oxidative stresses in tumours and for developing novel therapies based on the generation and exploitation of oxidative stress in cancer.

the oxidative stress generated in MCTS following the combination of certain chemotherapeutics and metabolic inhibitors is significantly higher than the individual drugs and is associated with the enhanced sensitivity of the MCTS to the combination therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MCTS are excellent in vitro models for understanding and designing therapies based on the generation and modulation of oxidative stress in the tumours.

the use of MCTS for developing therapies that are based upon the generation of mild to moderate levels ROS in the tumour, but not in the normal cells, may be a promising approach for the improvement of tumour therapy.

, the use of MCTS as in vitro models can provide a better understanding of the role of oxidative and nitrosative stress in treatment-induced cell death, which can lead to better design of therapies and therapeutics for the treatment of cancer.
